title: Quantum advantage in zero-error function computation with side information

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states "G \boxtimes H = G \lor H." This is false for the stated standard strong and OR products. In general, G \boxtimes H is a spanning subgraph of G \lor H, not equal to it. For example, let G=K_2 and let H be an edgeless graph on two vertices. In G \lor H, (g_1,h_1) and (g_2,h_2) are adjacent whenever g_1 and g_2 are adjacent, including when h_1 != h_2. In G \boxtimes H, they are not adjacent when h_1 != h_2 because the H coordinates are neither equal nor adjacent. The paper itself later uses the non-equality containment "G \boxtimes H \subseteq G \lor H" in Proposition 7, directly contradicting Proposition 1.

Under Definition 4, \xi(G) is defined using vectors orthogonal for non-adjacent vertices of G. Zero-error quantum communication instead requires states for adjacent vertices of the confusion graph G^{(m)} to be orthogonal. Therefore the relevant quantity is \xi(\overline{G^{(m)}}), not \xi(G^{(m)}). Lemma 4 nevertheless claims the optimum is "(log_2 \xi(G^{(m)}))/m" while its first line uses an orthogonal representation of \overline{G^{(m)}}. This is not a notational harmlessness: for an edgeless confusion graph on n>1 vertices, a zero-error protocol can send one fixed one-dimensional state, whereas \xi(G^{(m)}) under the paper's definition is n because every pair of vertices is non-adjacent and must be orthogonal. Thus the stated formula and Theorem 4 give the wrong quantum rate.

The converse takes "(x,x') \in E(\overline{G}^{(m)})" and concludes that a zero-error protocol requires \rho_x \perp \rho_{x'}. This reverses the required condition. An edge of the complement is a non-edge of the confusion graph, i.e. a pair that is not confusable and need not be distinguished by Bob. Zero-error requires orthogonality for edges of G^{(m)}, equivalently for non-edges of \overline{G^{(m)}}. The proof therefore does not establish the asserted orthogonal representation or lower bound.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section VI, proof of R_quantum(g), statement "C_5^{\vee m}=\overline{C_5^{\boxtimes m}}=C_5^{\boxtimes m}"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Self-complementarity of C_5 does imply (up to an isomorphism) \overline{C_5^{\boxtimes m}} \cong C_5^{\vee m}; it does not imply that C_5^{\boxtimes m} is self-complementary. For m=2, C_5^{\boxtimes 2} is 8-regular on 25 vertices, while C_5^{\vee 2}=\overline{C_5^{\boxtimes 2}} is 16-regular. Hence these graphs cannot be equal or isomorphic. The ensuing equality \xi(C_5^{\vee m})=\xi(C_5^{\boxtimes m}) and the transfer of the bound \xi(C_5^{\vee 2})\leq 5 to the strong-product graph are unjustified. This breaks the displayed proof of the quantum-rate conclusion, even if a corrected argument may be possible.

Theorem 2 claims a construction for every finite simple graph, but its proof sets \mathcal Y=E(G) and makes p_{XY}(x,y)>0 iff x is incident to y. If G has an isolated vertex, then p_{XY}(x,y)=0 for every y for that x, violating Assumption 1 and failing to define a source distribution with that x in its support. If G is edgeless, \mathcal Y is empty, so no joint pmf on X x Y can be defined at all. Thus the offered construction does not prove the theorem over the stated class of all finite simple graphs.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix proof labeled "Proof of (b)" for Theorem 1, paragraph beginning "Now let (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') \notin E(G^{\boxtimes m})"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The argument assumes all one-letter non-edges are C1 and correctly observes that a pair non-adjacent in the strong product has no jointly compatible y sequence, hence is non-adjacent in G^{(m)}. That establishes E(G^{(m)}) \subseteq E(G^{\boxtimes m}). Instead, the text concludes "Since (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') \notin E(G^{\vee m}) is arbitrary, this implies E(G^{\vee m}) \subseteq E(G^{(m)})". This changes the graph under discussion and reverses the implication. It does not prove either stated equality in that paragraph.

predicted_errors.error_location: Tables I–III and the associated claims in the paragraph beginning "The examples appear in Table I–III"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper's central examples f, g, and h are said to be specified in Tables I–III, but no such tables are present in the supplied paper. The inserted raster figures are labeled Figure 0 through Figure 3 and do not supply readable Tables I–III defining the functions or pmfs. Consequently the claims "G_f=G_g=G_h=C_5," "G_f^{(m)}=C_5^{\boxtimes m}," and "G_g^{(m)}=C_5^{\vee m}" cannot be checked from the document, and the later Section VI analysis refers to undefined table data.
